forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Greenwich ended 2025/26 with a £27.0m deficit on its dedicated schools grant
news_drafts.lead:
Greenwich ended 2025/26 with an accumulated deficit of £27.0m on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The figure is in the council's medium-term financial strategy, its financial plan for the coming years, which went to the council meeting of 21 October 2026. The paper says the deficit is "carried on the balance sheet".

The strategy refers to a statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet. It says the override excludes DSG deficits from the council's General Fund balances. The General Fund is the account paid for by council tax and business rates. The paper says the override is time-limited. It says the council could be required to fund all or part of the deficit if the override ceases without government intervention.

The paper also records that the government has announced proposals to fund up to 90% of historic high needs deficits. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The paper says details are still to be confirmed.

news_drafts.headline: Greenwich ended 2025/26 with a £27.0m schools-funding deficit; government proposes funding up to 90%
news_drafts.lead:
Greenwich ended 2025/26 with an accumulated deficit of £27.0m on the dedicated schools grant (DSG, the government grant that funds schools), carried on the council's balance sheet. The figure is in the council's medium-term financial strategy (MTFS, its financial plan for the next three to five years), which went to Cabinet on 21 October 2026.

A deficit on this grant is usually an overspend on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The paper says a statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, allows DSG deficits to be excluded from General Fund balances. It describes that override as time-limited.

The paper also notes the government's intention to address a substantial proportion of historic high needs deficits, including funding up to 90%. It says the detail, and how individual councils would be treated, are not yet confirmed. On that basis the paper does not give a figure for how much of Greenwich's £27.0m the proposal would cover.

news_drafts.headline: Greenwich schools funding deficit ended 2025/26 at £18.1m, with £16.0m on special needs support
news_drafts.lead:
Greenwich's schools funding ended the last financial year £18.1m in deficit, £5.9m more than the £12.2m forecast at the third-quarter check, according to the outturn report (the actual figures once a year has ended) before Cabinet on 23 September. Of that, £16.0m is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The deficit is on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools. The paper attributes £4.8m of the high needs shortfall to increased demand for independent SEND placements and £10.2m to "historical top up costs for special academies". A statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, runs until 2028. Relief depends on government approval of a "Local SEND Reform Plan" for a proposed High Needs Stability Grant covering 90%. The paper says: "Even if approved, the grant would not remove the ongoing financial risk." A budget monitoring appendix (the in-year check of spending against budget) shows a forecast £27.0m deficit against a budget of break-even.

SEND transport overspent by £1.5m. The paper says the number of children with Education, Health and Care Plans needing transport rose from 899 in the first quarter to 976 in the fourth, an increase of 8.5%. Between 2020/21 and 2025/26 the number of children carried rose from 767 to 850, and the cost per child from £16,607 to £22,513.

findings.headline: Rent convergence to formula rent could add £0.850m a year of HRA rental income from the 2028/29 increase
findings.detail: The Government announced rent convergence on 28 January 2026, at £1 a week from 2027/28 rising to £2 a week from 2028/29. The HRA estimate includes the full implementation. The paper says only 18% of HRA general needs properties are at formula rent, so about 16,000 homes are below formula rent.
findings.matters: Rent convergence is a national policy change with a per-home income effect that other social landlords with rents below formula would also face.
findings.figures: additional £0.850m rental income a year from the further £1 a week from 2028/29; 18% of HRA general needs properties at formula rent; c16,000 homes below formula rent
findings.quote: estimates are that this further £1 per week from 2028/29 could provide an additional £0.850m of rental income per year to the HRA.

findings.headline: The Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Direction, in place until 2030, is a potential opportunity with no financial benefit assumed
findings.detail: The paper says the council is identifying expenditure that could qualify for capital receipts to fund transformation revenue costs. Any proposals will go to Full Council once eligibility is confirmed. No benefit has been included in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Capital receipts used to fund transformation revenue costs would reduce the revenue budget pressure, and the eligibility decisions will be watched by other councils considering the same direction.
findings.figures: no amount assumed; direction in place until 2030
findings.quote: Whilst no financial benefit has been assumed at this stage

findings.headline: The Final 2026/27 settlement added £2.7m of Core Spending Power, mainly through Recovery Grant Uplift, not assumed beyond 2028/29
findings.detail: The paper says the additional funding was built into the 2026/27 service budgets. It is not assumed to continue after 2028/29, so its withdrawal increases the forecast gap in 2029/30. The Government's multi-year settlement is described as reducing uncertainty for 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.matters: Grant that is not assumed to continue creates a cliff-edge in later years, a pattern other councils relying on one-off grant uplifts would recognise.
findings.figures: additional Core Spending Power £2.7m for 2026/27; change in government funding assumptions (£0.3m) in 2027/28, (£1.1m) in 2028/29, £2.7m in 2029/30
findings.quote: An additional £2.7m of Core Spending Power (CSP) funding was confirmed through the Final Local Government Finance Settlement for 2026/27

findings.headline: The 2027/28 demand and non-pay inflation assumption falls to £17.3m from £26.3m
findings.detail: The paper says detailed modelling of Children's and Adult Social Care, with other service areas also reviewed, has reduced the assumed annual demand and inflation pressure. The revised profile is £17.3m in 2027/28, £20.6m in 2028/29 and £23.8m in 2029/30. The paper gives no further detail on the reduction.
findings.matters: A reduction of this size in the demand assumption is a material change to the forecast, and a peer council modelling the same services would want to know how it was derived.

findings.headline: The 2027/28 pay inflation assumption rises to £6.4m from £4.5m, based on a 3.3% annual pay award
findings.detail: The MTFS now provides for an annual 3.3% pay award from 2027/28, based on the 2026/27 national offer. The paper says the 2027/28 award is not yet confirmed and the assumption will be reviewed as negotiations progress.
findings.matters: A pay assumption set against an unagreed award shows the risk a finance director or lender would watch while the 2027/28 settlement is pending.
findings.quote: The MTFS assumptions have been updated to reflect a provision of an annual 3.3% pay award in 2027/28 and beyond.
